headline: Someone Looked at Five 500-Year-Old Trees and Thought 'I'll Take Those'
subheadline: *The centuries-old baobabs, intercepted en route to a mystery buyer in Georgia, are being replanted under cables and what staff describe as 'a profound sense of disappointment.'*
author: Busisiwe Nkosi, Horticultural Crimes Desk
seoTitle: South Africa Replants Smuggled Baobabs Bound for Georgia
seoDescription: Satire: Five 500-year-old baobabs were dug up in South Africa and nearly shipped to a mystery buyer in Georgia. The trees are being replanted and debriefed.
sourceEvent: Five centuries-old baobab trees weighing around 20 tonnes each were dug up in South Africa without the necessary permits by an exporter intending to ship them to an unnamed buyer in Georgia. After being intercepted in July and held at a Durban warehouse, the trees arrived at a reserve in Timbavati on Wednesday to be replanted and supported by cables.

social.x: Environmentalists are replanting five 500-year-old baobabs after a mystery buyer had them dug up for shipping to Georgia. The trees, older than most countries, are recovering under cables and, sources say, a deep sense of betrayal.

altHeadlines: Mystery Buyer Orders Five Ancient Trees as Though Ordering Curtains
Baobabs Older Than Most Countries Returned to Africa to Think About Nothing

body:
TIMBAVATI, SOUTH AFRICA — Environmentalists are racing to replant five centuries-old baobab trees after the 20-tonne specimens were dug up without permits and readied for shipment to Georgia, answering a question nobody had thought to ask: what happens if you simply take a tree?

The baobabs, each roughly 500 years old and therefore older than Georgia's current constitution, most European borders and the general concept of ordering things, arrived Wednesday at a reserve in Timbavati, where they will be supported by cables while they recover from what staff describe only as 'the incident.'

The trees had spent four months in a Durban warehouse after being intercepted in July, reportedly parked between a consignment of gym equipment and a pallet of garden furniture, in what officials called 'a paperwork discrepancy in the same way the Titanic had a hull discrepancy.'

The buyer, described on export documents as 'a private individual in Georgia,' remains unidentified. A customs official confirmed the description was accurate 'in the sense that it communicated literally nothing.' The manifest is said to have listed the contents as 'decorative landscaping items,' which is technically true of a tree in the same way the Crown Jewels are technically jewellery.

'It takes a special kind of confidence,' said one environmental analyst, 'to look at a living thing that survived the Little Ice Age, the Industrial Revolution and every single human conflict on record, and think: that would suit the driveway. And also that it fits in a box.'

Reserve staff said the trees were 'stable but furious,' a prognosis delivered by a spokesperson who conceded that baobabs cannot technically be furious 'but you'd reconsider if you'd seen the root balls.'

A warehouse worker who asked not to be named because he had grown attached said the baobabs had been 'perfect tenants' during their four-month stay. 'No noise, no complaints,' he said. 'One of them did lean about three degrees towards the exit, but I would too.'

Experts warned the recovery will be slow, noting that a tree alive for five centuries has a long memory. 'Baobabs store water, nutrients and, we believe, grudges,' said one botanist, who declined to elaborate, citing ongoing consultations with the trees.

A reserve spokesperson confirmed the support cables are there to help the baobabs re-establish, 'and, if we're honest, to make it marginally harder for them to be ordered online again.'

Authorities declined to say whether charges will be filed, noting the case raises novel legal questions, including whether a 500-year-old tree counts as a witness and, if so, whether it can be compelled to testify.

At press time, the unnamed buyer had reportedly submitted a new enquiry, this time about a mountain.
